reading.body:
The Business Roundtable's AI lobbying runs through one client, 17 filings, and a roster of 26 named lobbyists, with two bills named.

The structure is a single client with a deep bench. Seventeen filings name the same client, and ten lobbyists appear on all 17 of them. That is not a broad portfolio of AI clients. It is one organization's AI agenda carried by a stable core of people, with a tail of 16 more lobbyists appearing on between one and 14 filings each. The counts measure disclosure volume, not influence or spending.

For AI specifically, this is the trade-association pattern rather than the single-company pattern. The Business Roundtable is a membership body, so its filings aggregate the AI positions of large employers into one LDA registrant. The two bills named, HR 633 and S 146, are the only legislative targets the data identifies, and both are tied to filings from 2025 or later. Nothing here says what the Roundtable argued, only that it reported lobbying on AI.

What the data does not cover is the substance. It has no dollar amounts, no agency targets, no filing dates, and no text of the positions taken. It also does not connect this lobbying to data centers, power procurement, or grid policy, so any claim that these filings concern compute buildout would be an addition, not a reading. The counts also cannot distinguish a lobbyist who worked a file from one listed for administrative completeness.
